title: Se fue la luz
desc: The power goes out and the pulpería is dark
setting: It is eight at night and the whole block goes dark at once. You walk to doña Chepa's pulpería with your phone in your hand.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.es: Ideay, se fue la luz otra vez. ¿Qué andás buscando?
steps.en: Ideay, the power has gone again. What are you after?

options.en: Evening, doña. Do you sell candles?
options.feedback: Right on both counts - you greeted her first, and candela is the word here for a candle.
She will work it out, but you have asked her for light rather than for a candle.
Nothing to do with the blackout. Read the moment.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.en: I have some. How many do you want?

options.feedback: Deme is exactly how you ask for something across a counter here.
Understood, but bare. One word to a neighbour sounds short.
She cannot help you decide. Pick a number.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.en: Here you go. That is twenty córdobas.

options.en: Thank you, doña. Do you know until what time?
options.feedback: Thanks first, then the one question the whole block wants answered. That is what a counter is for.
Polite and correct. You just missed a chance to keep her talking.
Twenty córdobas for two is normal, and complaining to a neighbour costs you more than the money.

steps.speaker: Doña Chepa
steps.es: Dicen que como a las once. Cuidado con el fuego, mijo.
steps.en: They say about eleven. Careful with the fire, son.

options.es: Va pues, doña. Que pase buena noche.
options.en: Right then, doña. Have a good night.
options.feedback: Va pues is the Nicaraguan sign-off, and you wished her the night back.
Adiós sounds like forever here. Save it for somebody leaving the country.

options.es: No hay problema, yo sé de fuego.
options.en: No problem, I know about fire.
options.feedback: She was looking after you. Brushing it off is not the way to take it.
